title: India's Food Regulator to Take Bisleri to Court Over Unsafe Water Sample
excerpt: The FSSAI sanctioned prosecution after one lab found a Bisleri packaged-water sample over bromate limits and a referral lab, on the company's own appeal, detected PAHs and also declared it unsafe.
body:
• India's food safety regulator, the FSSAI, said on Sunday it has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a regulatory sample of its packaged drinking water was declared unsafe.
  • A first laboratory found the sample non-compliant with prescribed bromate limits; after Bisleri appealed, a referral laboratory also declared it unsafe, detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
  • For readers: a sanction to prosecute is permission to launch court proceedings under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 — it is not a court verdict, and Bisleri had not responded to Reuters' request for comment outside business hours.
  • The same FSSAI action covered four other companies — Vasant Masala, Tit-Bit Foods, Asha Confectionery and Mimansa Industries — over samples found unsafe for various violations.

India's food safety regulator will take Bisleri International, maker of the country's best-known bottled water brand, to court after a sample of its packaged drinking water was found to be unsafe, Reuters reported on Sunday.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said a regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from Bisleri's premises for analysis. The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed limits for bromate — a chemical formed as a by-product of certain disinfection processes — and was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Bisleri appealed against the initial finding, as the Act allows. The sample was then sent to a Referral Food Laboratory, which also declared it unsafe, this time after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs.

"The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the FSS Act, 2006. Sanction has been granted to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd," the FSSAI said. Bisleri did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours, Reuters reported.

Part of a wider enforcement round

Bisleri was not the only company named on Sunday. According to The Hindu BusinessLine, the FSSAI also sanctioned prosecution against Vasant Masala Pvt Ltd, whose chilli powder sample was found unsafe even by the referral lab; Tit-Bit Foods (India) Pvt Ltd, whose pre-packaged turmeric powder and chilli powder samples were found unsafe due to pesticide residues exceeding permissible limits; Mimansa Industries Pvt Ltd, over a sample of walnut kernels found unsafe; and Asha Confectionery, for various violations.

Reuters noted that the regulator has stepped up enforcement against major brands this year, including legal action against Nestlé over a baby food sample it found substandard in September. Bisleri competes with PepsiCo's Aquafina and Coca-Cola's Kinley in India's packaged drinking water market, which Persistence Market Research valued at $3.6 billion in 2025.

What this does and does not mean

Two limits on the finding matter for anyone reading the headline at a shop shelf. First, the reported finding concerns the regulatory sample the FSSAI tested — tested twice, by two laboratories, with two different substances cited — and the regulator's public statement, as reported, does not name a batch or announce a recall. Second, a sanction for prosecution starts a legal process; it is not a finding of guilt, and Bisleri has yet to state its position publicly. What happens next is a court case in which the company can contest the laboratory findings it has already appealed once through the referral process.

What's next

The prosecution will proceed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. For the regulator, the Bisleri case is the most prominent in a year of visibly tougher enforcement against large food brands. For Bisleri — a name so established in India that it is often used generically for bottled water — the case will test how a market leader responds when the challenge is not a competitor's claim but its own regulator's laboratory results.
